title: The Competitive Firm's Supply Curve
short: Maximize pq − C(q): set p = MC on the rising part of MC above minimum average variable cost.
trouble: Students take the whole MC curve as the supply curve, including its falling part and the part below minimum AVC.

blocks.html: A competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it likes at the market price $p$, and nothing above it. The Shutdown Rule told it when to stay open; with a cost function and Where Average Cost Is Lowest we can derive its whole supply curve.

A price taker maximizes $\pi(q) = pq - C(q)$. It produces where $$p = MC(q)$$ on the rising part of marginal cost, as long as $p$ is at least the minimum of average variable cost. Below that price it produces nothing. Its short-run supply curve is the part of $MC$ above minimum $AVC$.

First-order condition: $\pi'(q) = p - C'(q) = 0$. Second-order condition: $\pi''(q) = -C''(q) < 0$, so marginal cost must be rising; where MC is falling, $p = MC$ marks a profit minimum. Then compare with shutting down: producing gives $pq - VC(q) - F$, shutting down gives $-F$ (the fixed cost is owed either way in the short run). Producing is better exactly when $pq \ge VC(q)$, that is, $p \ge AVC(q)$.

blocks.name: ec-costcurves

opts.task: Move the price below \$7.50 and watch output drop to zero.

blocks.cap: $C(q) = 100 + 10q - q^2 + 0.1q^3$. The thick part of MC, above minimum AVC (\$7.50 at $q = 5$), is the supply curve. At \$20 the firm makes 10 units and just breaks even.

blocks.title: A simple cost function
steps: $AVC = q$ is always below $MC$, so any positive price keeps it producing. Supply: $q = p/2$.

blocks.title: A cubic cost function
steps: Revenue 200, cost $100 + 100 - 100 + 100 = 200$: zero economic profit. \$20 is the bottom of ATC.

blocks.title: Below the shutdown price
blocks.q: Same firm, but the price falls to \$7.
steps: \$7 is below that, so every unit produced loses money on top of the fixed cost. Output: 0, loss \$100 (the fixed cost).

blocks.html: Market supply in the short run is the horizontal sum of the firms' supply curves, the same adding-up as Adding Up to Market Demand: with 50 firms that each supply $q = p/2$, the market supplies $Q = 25p$. Each firm's curve starts at its own shutdown price, so the market curve has a step or kink wherever a group of firms enters.

Taking the whole MC curve as the supply curve. The falling part of MC is where $p = MC$ gives a profit minimum, and the part below minimum AVC is where the firm would rather shut down. Check: at your quantity, MC must be rising and the price must be at least AVC.
